screens.title: Smart Contract Vulnerabilities — Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contract vulnerabilities are code-level mistakes that can directly affect on-chain assets. Because blockchain transactions are immutable, any bug that changes balances, transfers funds, or enables unauthorized calls can cause permanent loss. The most common categories include reentrancy, where external calls allow repeated control flow back into a contract; front-running, where attackers reorder transactions for profit; integer overflow and underflow, where arithmetic exceeds type bounds; access control lapses that expose privileged functions; and denial-of-service conditions that make contract functions unusable. Each class of vulnerability has a clear behavioral signature and corresponding mitigation. For example, reentrancy often appears when a contract makes an external call before updating internal balances; the fix is to update state first and then interact, and to consider reentrancy guards. Front-running shows up when actions are sensitive to transaction ordering; commit-reveal or time-locks reduce that sensitivity. Integer bugs are either solved by using a modern compiler with built-in checks or by using a safe arithmetic library in older versions. The key takeaway is that vulnerabilities are not abstract — they are specific code patterns you can detect, automate against, and design around. A security-first mindset treats each external call, dependency, and user input as untrusted, and builds checks into the simplest operations.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Smart Contract Vulnerabilities
Vulnerability Categories
Recognize these patterns in contract code and design.
Reentrancy — external call before state update
Front-running — mempool observation and reorder
Integer overflow/underflow — arithmetic outside type bounds
Access control — insufficient role checks
Denial of Service — unbounded loops or blocked execution
Key Takeaway

Vulnerabilities are predictable patterns. Automate detection and architect contracts so unsafe actions are difficult to trigger.

Common-mistake highlight

Developers often trust that a call to an address is harmless. The mistake is assuming no code runs on the other side. Treat external calls as potential entry points for state changes.

Concrete example
A withdraw function that sends funds and only later decrements a balance enables repeated withdrawals by a malicious contract that re-enters the function.
Misconception
Assuming gas costs or network conditions will stop an attack is unreliable.
Pro tip
Make state changes before interactions and consider nonReentrant guards for critical functions.

screens.title: Reentrancy Attack — Vulnerable Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Reentrancy occurs when a contract makes an external call before finishing state updates, enabling the callee to re-enter the original function and alter state unexpectedly. In the provided vulnerable bank example the contract sends Ether to msg. sender and only after that reduces the sender's balance. A malicious contract can deposit, then call withdraw to trigger an external transfer. When the bank calls back into the attacker through the fallback or receive function, the attacker calls withdraw again before the balance is decremented, withdrawing more than deposited. The practical lab shows two contracts: the vulnerable bank and an attack contract that repeatedly re-enters the withdraw flow until the bank is drained. When you read the vulnerable contract, look for the order of operations: require checks, external call, then state updates. That ordering is the root cause. A key misconception is assuming modern Solidity always prevents reentrancy; even with a modern compiler, developer ordering still matters. The code walkthrough below is the exact pattern to identify during audits and code review. As a learner, when you see an external call to an untrusted address, flag the function for deeper inspection.

keyIdea.text: External calls before state updates allow re-entry and repeated operations; order of operations is the vulnerability.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Reentrancy: Vulnerable Code
VulnerableBank.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableBank {
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

  function deposit() public payable {
    balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  }

  function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Withdrawal failed");

    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // state update happens after external call
  }
}
Look for the external call to msg.sender before the balance decrement. That ordering enables reentrant calls.
Attack.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

interface IBank { function deposit() external payable; function withdraw(uint256) external; }

contract Attack {
  IBank public bank;
  address public owner;

  constructor(address _bankAddress) { bank = IBank(_bankAddress); owner = msg.sender; }

  function attack() public payable {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can attack");
    bank.deposit{value: msg.value}();
    bank.withdraw(msg.value);
  }

  receive() external payable {
    if (address(bank).balance >= 0.001 ether) {
      bank.withdraw(0.001 ether);
    }
  }
}
Concrete scenario
An attacker deposits and triggers withdraw; their fallback re-enters withdraw repeatedly until funds drain.
Check your understanding
If a function calls an external contract, what should you verify about the operation order?

screens.title: Mitigating Reentrancy — Checks‑Effects‑Interactions
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable mitigation pattern for reentrancy is Checks-Effects-Interactions. The pattern dictates you perform all input validation first, then update the contract's own state, and only after that make external calls. Moving the state update before the external call prevents a re-entering contract from observing stale state and repeating the action. Additionally, using a reentrancy guard makes the function non-reentrant by ensuring it cannot be entered while it is already running. The lab shows SecureBank that applies both techniques: it decrements the caller's balance before sending Ether and uses a nonReentrant modifier from a trusted library. While the nonReentrant modifier is an added safety net, the order of operations is the primary correction. A common misconception is relying solely on low-level gas constraints to prevent reentry; this is brittle because gas costs and execution contexts change. After applying these fixes, redeploying and re-running the attack should fail because the attacker cannot withdraw twice in a single call. Always treat external calls as risky and prefer pull-based flows where beneficiaries withdraw funds themselves rather than having the contract push payments in loops.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Mitigating Reentrancy
SecureBank.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/security/ReentrancyGuard.sol";

contract SecureBank is ReentrancyGuard {
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

  function deposit() public payable { balances[msg.sender] += msg.value; }

  function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public nonReentrant {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");
    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // Effects first
    (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
  }
}
Notice the balance change before the external call and the nonReentrant modifier for extra protection.
Best practices checklist
  • Update internal state before external calls.
  • Use nonReentrant guards where state changes and external interactions occur.
  • Favor pull payments over push payments for multiple recipients.
  • Audit all public and external functions for reentrancy entry points.
Misconception
Relying on low gas stipends of transfer/send is not a robust defense strategy across EVM forks and future gas rules.

screens.title: Front-running and Order-Dependence
screens.narratorSegment: Front-running occurs when an attacker observes a pending transaction in the mempool and then submits a competing transaction with a higher gas price to get included first. This is common in decentralized exchanges and NFT minting where order impacts asset allocation or price. The root cause is a contract or dApp that lets transaction order change outcomes in a way that benefits someone who sees pending transactions. Mitigations include designing contracts to be less order-sensitive, using commit-reveal schemes so the critical action is revealed only after a commit phase, or adding time-locks that make instant reorderings ineffective. A simple commit-reveal makes attackers unable to learn intent before committing because they only see a hashed commitment. Time-locks and batched processing reduce sensitivity to single-transaction ordering by applying operations in a fixed window. A common misconception is thinking front-running is only a miner problem; it can also be performed by any node or MEV bot observing the mempool. When evaluating a contract, ask whether knowing an in-flight transaction gives an attacker a direct profit opportunity. If so, add a protocol-level guard such as commit-reveal or batch settlement.

How front-running works
Mempool visibility lets attackers observe and reorder transactions by paying for priority inclusion.
Observe pending transaction
Submit higher-fee transaction to be mined earlier

screens.title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
screens.narratorSegment: Integer overflow and underflow happen when arithmetic results exceed the representable range of a numeric type. In EVM contracts, unsigned integers wrap around in older compilers, causing unexpected large values or silent failures. For example, subtracting from zero could produce a huge number in wrapped arithmetic. These bugs can be exploited in balance calculations and supply arithmetic. Modern Solidity versions, starting at 0.8.0, include automatic checks that revert on overflow or underflow, eliminating many classes of errors. For older contracts, developers used safe arithmetic libraries that explicitly check and revert on bad arithmetic. When auditing, verify the compiler version and whether SafeMath or equivalent is used. Misconceptions include thinking overflow cannot happen if values are small in tests; real users and composable contracts may produce edge values you never expected. The practical guidance is to use Solidity 0.8.0 or later for new code, add explicit checks on critical math, and include unit tests that exercise boundary conditions so arithmetic faults are caught during development rather than on-chain. Integer Overflow and Underflow means prefer solidity 0.8+ with built-in arithmetic checks; test boundary conditions and avoid silent wraparound semantics.. In practical terms, how arithmetic errors arise and modern safeguards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Why it matters
Incorrect arithmetic can alter balances or token supplies, enabling theft or logic bypass.

Check your tests

screens.title: Access Control Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Access control prevents unauthorized users from calling privileged functions. Common patterns include an owner-only modifier for single-administrator contracts and role-based access control for more flexible systems where many roles exist such as admin, pauser, or minter. The main design principle is least privilege: grant only the permissions necessary for a role to operate. Effective access control requires clear initialization, migration paths for role changes, and careful handling of contract ownership transfers. Mistakes include leaving functions public that alter important parameters or assuming that only externally owned accounts will call a function; contracts can be called by other contracts which may chain privileged calls. Use battle-tested libraries that implement RBAC and ownership transfer safety checks. When designing your architecture, separate governance operations from runtime funds logic where possible, and include emergency pause controls to mitigate a discovered exploit without immediately breaking the system. Audit role assignment flows, especially those triggered during initialization or upgrade operations, because these are frequent sources of mistakes. Owner, multi-role RBAC, and emergency pausers are common building blocks.

Role-based access control: assign multiple granular permissions

Design checks

  • Keep governance actions distinct from funds transfers.
Combining clear access control with pause mechanisms and upgrade-safe patterns reduces blast radius when a bug appears.

screens.title: Denial of Service (DoS) Risks
screens.narratorSegment: Denial of service in smart contracts can take several forms: making a function too expensive to run due to unbounded loops, allowing a single account to block progress, or relying on external services that can fail. A common pattern is iterating over a growing array of user addresses in a single transaction; as the list grows, the gas required exceeds block limits and the function becomes unusable. Another DoS vector is making assumptions about successful external calls without fallback behavior. The defenses are straightforward: avoid unbounded iteration in on-chain flows, use pull-based payment models so recipients withdraw funds on their own schedule, and design for failure by handling unsuccessful calls gracefully. Rate-limiting, batching work across multiple transactions, and delegating heavy computation off-chain are also practical mitigations. A typical misconception is assuming rare worst-case sizes won't matter; production systems see scale, so architect for growth. The operational takeaway is to test contract methods against large dataset simulations and prefer patterns that keep per-transaction gas bounded and predictable. narration.text: Denial of service in smart contracts can take several forms: making a function too expensive to run due to unbounded loops, allowing a single account to block progress, or relying on external services that can fail. A common pattern is iterating over a growing array of user addresses in a single transaction; as the list grows, the gas required exceeds block limits and the function becomes unusable. Another DoS vector is making assumptions about successful external calls without fallback behavior. The defenses are straightforward: avoid unbounded iteration in on-chain flows, use pull-based payment models so recipients withdraw funds on their own schedule, and design for failure by handling unsuccessful calls gracefully. Rate-limiting, batching work across multiple transactions, and delegating heavy computation off-chain are also practical mitigations. A typical misconception is assuming rare worst-case sizes won't matter; production systems see scale, so architect for growth. The operational takeaway is to test contract methods against large dataset simulations and prefer patterns that keep per-transaction gas bounded and predictable. Denial of Service (DoS)
Design contracts so core functions cannot be blocked by scale or single accounts.
Problem examples

screens.title: Client-side Security — XSS and Private Keys
screens.narratorSegment: Frontend security mistakes often undermine on-chain protections. Cross-site scripting allows an attacker to inject scripts into your dApp UI, which can then trigger wallet prompts or manipulate transaction data. If your UI renders user-generated content without proper sanitation, attackers can craft payloads that change the transaction details a user sees or overlay fake wallet prompts. React escapes content by default, but using dangerouslySetInnerHTML or rendering raw H T M L is a common source of XSS. The other critical frontend risk is private key exposure: never ask users for their private keys or store them in browser storage. The correct model is to direct all signing operations to wallet providers so the key material never leaves the wallet. A common misconception is that storing encrypted keys in local storage is safe; browsers are not secure vaults, and an XSS flaw can reveal secrets. The practical guidance: sanitize or avoid rendering raw H T M L, minimize the data you show in an untrusted context, and always use wallet APIs for signing. Communicate clearly to users what they are signing so they can spot suspicious requests.

Sanitize or avoid rendering raw HTML. Treat any user content as untrusted.

An attacker injects a script that modifies displayed transaction amounts or triggers a malicious signing request in the UI.

screens.title: Dependency Vulnerabilities & Phishing
screens.narratorSegment: Dependencies are a common source of vulnerabilities. Malicious or vulnerable npm packages can be introduced unintentionally or by supply-chain attacks. Regularly run dependency audits and updates, use automated tools that flag known issues, and minimize the number of direct dependencies in critical systems. Tools that report vulnerabilities let you triage and patch known problems before they reach production. On the social side, phishing and spoofing target users rather than code. Attackers create fake dApps or copy interfaces to trick users into revealing seed phrases or signing harmful transactions. Enforce HTTPS, educate users to check domains, and make wallet prompts explicit and human-readable so users can verify what they are signing. A good misconception to highlight is thinking that technical defenses alone are sufficient; user education and clear UX are part of the security fabric. Combine dependency hygiene with user-facing protections to reduce both technical and human risks. screens.title: Security Audits and Tooling
screens.narratorSegment: Audits combine automated tooling with expert manual review. Automated tools catch many common patterns quickly: static analyzers look for code smells and likely bugs, symbolic execution can find complex stateful faults, and dynamic analysis explores runtime behavior. Examples of tools used in practice include static analysis frameworks that detect known vulnerability patterns and analysis platforms that combine multiple methods to surface issues. In addition to automated checks, a professional manual audit reviews design assumptions, threat models, and edge cases that tooling may miss. Use well-audited libraries such as trusted contract suites to avoid implementing common components yourself. A practical workflow is to run automated tools early in CI, then run a manual audit before mainnet deployment, and finally apply fixes and re-run automation to confirm resolution. Misconceptions include assuming that tooling alone guarantees safety; tools help find issues but do not replace a careful design review. The operational advice is to integrate analysis into your development lifecycle and to rely on community-vetted building blocks where possible to reduce the chance of introducing repeatable mistakes. screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Reentrancy Lab

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the compact concepts you should carry into design and audits. Reentrancy is the pattern where external calls allow repeated entry into a function and is prevented by ordering state updates before interactions and by using reentrancy guards. Front-running is an order-dependence exploit where attackers observe the mempool and reorder transactions; commit-reveal and batching reduce this sensitivity. Integer overflow and underflow are arithmetic faults avoidable by using modern compiler checks or safe arithmetic libraries. These six items are the most actionable starting points for secure dApp development: spot these patterns, apply the appropriate mitigation, incorporate tools in CI, and educate users through clear UX. When in doubt, treat external input and calls as untrusted and prefer the simplest, most conservative handling of funds. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we take a practical, security-first look at decentralized applications. Blockchains make transactions immutable and irreversible, so a single vulnerability in a contract or the dApp frontend can cause permanent financial loss. You will learn to recognize common smart contract flaws such as reentrancy, front-running, and integer arithmetic bugs, and you will see how frontend risks like cross-site scripting and private key exposure make otherwise-safe contracts dangerous in practice. We will also cover auditing workflows and tools that give you automated and manual checks before deployment, and user-facing practices that reduce social engineering risk. This chapter finishes with a hands-on lab where you will analyze a vulnerable bank contract, run an attack from a second contract, and then apply the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and a reentrancy guard to fix it. Throughout, the emphasis is defensive design: assume malicious input, minimize trust, and make unsafe actions hard rather than easy. By the end you won't just know patterns; you'll be able to choose tools and processes that reduce the attack surface and protect users' funds.

These objectives orient your study and give measurable outcomes. First, you will be able to identify common smart contract vulnerabilities, such as reentrancy, front-running, integer overflow, access control gaps, and denial-of-service patterns. Identifying these mistakes is the first step to reducing risk. Second, you will understand dApp frontend risks, specifically cross-site scripting and how poor handling of private keys or wallet prompts can lead to fund loss. That knowledge helps you design safer UX and minimize attack surface. Third, you will learn about auditing tools and methodologies used today, including static analysis and symbolic execution platforms, plus community-vetted libraries that reduce repeatable mistakes. Finally, you will implement best practices for user education and wallet security within a dApp, so users see clear transaction details and know not to share seed phrases. Each objective is framed so you can measure competency: recognize patterns, explain mitigations, run tooling, and change UX behavior to reduce user risk.

These applied milestones help you measure progress while building. First, cultivate a security-first mindset: treating every external call and user input as untrusted and designing contracts so state updates happen before external interactions. Second, reinforce private key protection by never requesting seed phrases, avoiding browser storage for secrets, and always directing signing to wallet providers. Third, integrate dependency monitoring and update workflows so known vulnerabilities in packages do not become dApp vulnerabilities. Lastly, run an audit workflow that combines automated static analysis with a professional manual review and use vetted libraries where possible. Together these milestones move you from theory to repeatable practice: the goal is not just to know the patterns but to make them part of your CI/CD and user flows so mistakes are caught early and users are protected during runtime.

Smart contract vulnerabilities are code-level mistakes that can directly affect on-chain assets. Because blockchain transactions are immutable, any bug that changes balances, transfers funds, or enables unauthorized calls can cause permanent loss. The most common categories include reentrancy, where external calls allow repeated control flow back into a contract; front-running, where attackers reorder transactions for profit; integer overflow and underflow, where arithmetic exceeds type bounds; access control lapses that expose privileged functions; and denial-of-service conditions that make contract functions unusable. Each class of vulnerability has a clear behavioral signature and corresponding mitigation. For example, reentrancy often appears when a contract makes an external call before updating internal balances; the fix is to update state first and then interact, and to consider reentrancy guards. Front-running shows up when actions are sensitive to transaction ordering; commit-reveal or time-locks reduce that sensitivity. Integer bugs are either solved by using a modern compiler with built-in checks or by using a safe arithmetic library in older versions. The key takeaway is that vulnerabilities are not abstract — they are specific code patterns you can detect, automate against, and design around. A security-first mindset treats each external call, dependency, and user input as untrusted, and builds checks into the simplest operations.

Reentrancy occurs when a contract makes an external call before finishing state updates, enabling the callee to re-enter the original function and alter state unexpectedly. In the provided vulnerable bank example the contract sends Ether to msg. sender and only after that reduces the sender's balance. A malicious contract can deposit, then call withdraw to trigger an external transfer. When the bank calls back into the attacker through the fallback or receive function, the attacker calls withdraw again before the balance is decremented, withdrawing more than deposited. The practical lab shows two contracts: the vulnerable bank and an attack contract that repeatedly re-enters the withdraw flow until the bank is drained. When you read the vulnerable contract, look for the order of operations: require checks, external call, then state updates. That ordering is the root cause. A key misconception is assuming modern Solidity always prevents reentrancy; even with a modern compiler, developer ordering still matters. The code walkthrough below is the exact pattern to identify during audits and code review. As a learner, when you see an external call to an untrusted address, flag the function for deeper inspection.

A reliable mitigation pattern for reentrancy is Checks-Effects-Interactions. The pattern dictates you perform all input validation first, then update the contract's own state, and only after that make external calls. Moving the state update before the external call prevents a re-entering contract from observing stale state and repeating the action. Additionally, using a reentrancy guard makes the function non-reentrant by ensuring it cannot be entered while it is already running. The lab shows SecureBank that applies both techniques: it decrements the caller's balance before sending Ether and uses a nonReentrant modifier from a trusted library. While the nonReentrant modifier is an added safety net, the order of operations is the primary correction. A common misconception is relying solely on low-level gas constraints to prevent reentry; this is brittle because gas costs and execution contexts change. After applying these fixes, redeploying and re-running the attack should fail because the attacker cannot withdraw twice in a single call. Always treat external calls as risky and prefer pull-based flows where beneficiaries withdraw funds themselves rather than having the contract push payments in loops.

Front-running occurs when an attacker observes a pending transaction in the mempool and then submits a competing transaction with a higher gas price to get included first. This is common in decentralized exchanges and NFT minting where order impacts asset allocation or price. The root cause is a contract or dApp that lets transaction order change outcomes in a way that benefits someone who sees pending transactions. Mitigations include designing contracts to be less order-sensitive, using commit-reveal schemes so the critical action is revealed only after a commit phase, or adding time-locks that make instant reorderings ineffective. A simple commit-reveal makes attackers unable to learn intent before committing because they only see a hashed commitment. Time-locks and batched processing reduce sensitivity to single-transaction ordering by applying operations in a fixed window. A common misconception is thinking front-running is only a miner problem; it can also be performed by any node or MEV bot observing the mempool. When evaluating a contract, ask whether knowing an in-flight transaction gives an attacker a direct profit opportunity. If so, add a protocol-level guard such as commit-reveal or batch settlement.

Integer overflow and underflow happen when arithmetic results exceed the representable range of a numeric type. In EVM contracts, unsigned integers wrap around in older compilers, causing unexpected large values or silent failures. For example, subtracting from zero could produce a huge number in wrapped arithmetic. These bugs can be exploited in balance calculations and supply arithmetic. Modern Solidity versions, starting at 0.8.0, include automatic checks that revert on overflow or underflow, eliminating many classes of errors. For older contracts, developers used safe arithmetic libraries that explicitly check and revert on bad arithmetic. When auditing, verify the compiler version and whether SafeMath or equivalent is used. Misconceptions include thinking overflow cannot happen if values are small in tests; real users and composable contracts may produce edge values you never expected. The practical guidance is to use Solidity 0.8.0 or later for new code, add explicit checks on critical math, and include unit tests that exercise boundary conditions so arithmetic faults are caught during development rather than on-chain. Integer Overflow and Underflow means prefer solidity 0.8+ with built-in arithmetic checks; test boundary conditions and avoid silent wraparound semantics.. In practical terms, how arithmetic errors arise and modern safeguards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Access control prevents unauthorized users from calling privileged functions. Common patterns include an owner-only modifier for single-administrator contracts and role-based access control for more flexible systems where many roles exist such as admin, pauser, or minter. The main design principle is least privilege: grant only the permissions necessary for a role to operate. Effective access control requires clear initialization, migration paths for role changes, and careful handling of contract ownership transfers. Mistakes include leaving functions public that alter important parameters or assuming that only externally owned accounts will call a function; contracts can be called by other contracts which may chain privileged calls. Use battle-tested libraries that implement RBAC and ownership transfer safety checks. When designing your architecture, separate governance operations from runtime funds logic where possible, and include emergency pause controls to mitigate a discovered exploit without immediately breaking the system. Audit role assignment flows, especially those triggered during initialization or upgrade operations, because these are frequent sources of mistakes. Access Control Patterns means apply least privilege, use audited rbac libraries, and separate governance from runtime funds to reduce risk.. In practical terms, designing role checks and least-privilege boundaries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Denial of service in smart contracts can take several forms: making a function too expensive to run due to unbounded loops, allowing a single account to block progress, or relying on external services that can fail. A common pattern is iterating over a growing array of user addresses in a single transaction; as the list grows, the gas required exceeds block limits and the function becomes unusable. Another DoS vector is making assumptions about successful external calls without fallback behavior. The defenses are straightforward: avoid unbounded iteration in on-chain flows, use pull-based payment models so recipients withdraw funds on their own schedule, and design for failure by handling unsuccessful calls gracefully. Rate-limiting, batching work across multiple transactions, and delegating heavy computation off-chain are also practical mitigations. A typical misconception is assuming rare worst-case sizes won't matter; production systems see scale, so architect for growth. Frontend security mistakes often undermine on-chain protections. Cross-site scripting allows an attacker to inject scripts into your dApp UI, which can then trigger wallet prompts or manipulate transaction data. If your UI renders user-generated content without proper sanitation, attackers can craft payloads that change the transaction details a user sees or overlay fake wallet prompts. React escapes content by default, but using dangerouslySetInnerHTML or rendering raw H T M L is a common source of XSS. The other critical frontend risk is private key exposure: never ask users for their private keys or store them in browser storage. The correct model is to direct all signing operations to wallet providers so the key material never leaves the wallet. A common misconception is that storing encrypted keys in local storage is safe; browsers are not secure vaults, and an XSS flaw can reveal secrets. The practical guidance: sanitize or avoid rendering raw H T M L, minimize the data you show in an untrusted context, and always use wallet APIs for signing. Communicate clearly to users what they are signing so they can spot suspicious requests.

Dependencies are a common source of vulnerabilities. Malicious or vulnerable npm packages can be introduced unintentionally or by supply-chain attacks. Regularly run dependency audits and updates, use automated tools that flag known issues, and minimize the number of direct dependencies in critical systems. Tools that report vulnerabilities let you triage and patch known problems before they reach production. On the social side, phishing and spoofing target users rather than code. Attackers create fake dApps or copy interfaces to trick users into revealing seed phrases or signing harmful transactions. Enforce HTTPS, educate users to check domains, and make wallet prompts explicit and human-readable so users can verify what they are signing. A good misconception to highlight is thinking that technical defenses alone are sufficient; user education and clear UX are part of the security fabric. Combine dependency hygiene with user-facing protections to reduce both technical and human risks. Audits combine automated tooling with expert manual review. Automated tools catch many common patterns quickly: static analyzers look for code smells and likely bugs, symbolic execution can find complex stateful faults, and dynamic analysis explores runtime behavior. Examples of tools used in practice include static analysis frameworks that detect known vulnerability patterns and analysis platforms that combine multiple methods to surface issues. In addition to automated checks, a professional manual audit reviews design assumptions, threat models, and edge cases that tooling may miss. Use well-audited libraries such as trusted contract suites to avoid implementing common components yourself. A practical workflow is to run automated tools early in CI, then run a manual audit before mainnet deployment, and finally apply fixes and re-run automation to confirm resolution. Misconceptions include assuming that tooling alone guarantees safety; tools help find issues but do not replace a careful design review. The operational advice is to integrate analysis into your development lifecycle and to rely on community-vetted building blocks where possible to reduce the chance of introducing repeatable mistakes. Here are the compact concepts you should carry into design and audits. Reentrancy is the pattern where external calls allow repeated entry into a function and is prevented by ordering state updates before interactions and by using reentrancy guards. Front-running is an order-dependence exploit where attackers observe the mempool and reorder transactions; commit-reveal and batching reduce this sensitivity. Integer overflow and underflow are arithmetic faults avoidable by using modern compiler checks or safe arithmetic libraries. These six items are the most actionable starting points for secure dApp development: spot these patterns, apply the appropriate mitigation, incorporate tools in CI, and educate users through clear UX. When in doubt, treat external input and calls as untrusted and prefer the simplest, most conservative handling of funds. Secure dApp development includes client-side protections and disciplined audit practices. First, XSS can turn safe contracts into dangerous UX; sanitize or avoid raw H T M L and ensure transaction details are shown inside the wallet where users can verify them. Second, private keys must never be requested or stored by the dApp; always use wallet providers for signing and make network and transaction details explicit. Third, an effective audit combines automated static and dynamic analysis with a manual expert review and the use of audited libraries. Finally, user education and clear interface design reduce social-engineering risk. The practical memory here is to protect both the code and the user: tools will find many issues, but the last line of defense is careful UX and user training. Ask yourself before each release: would a beginner understand what they are signing, and could an external call be exploited for reentry or ordering attacks?
